claim: Globular bushy cells (GBCs) in the anteroventral cochlear nucleus (aVCN) project long axons approximately 3 mm to form monosynaptic calyx synapses onto principal cells in the contralateral medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB).
source: Globular bushy cells (GBCs) in anteroventral cochlear nucleus (aVCN) project long axons (~3 mm) forming monosynaptic calyx synapses onto principal cells in the contralateral medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the anatomical pathway.

claim: At postnatal day 8 (P8), the calyx of Held largely surrounds the postsynaptic neuron with a spherical or spoon-shaped morphology.
source: Up to approximately postnatal day (P) 12, the calyx primarily has a spherical or spoon-shaped morphology (Figure 1B, left panels).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B left panels with VGLUT1 labeling at P8.

claim: By postnatal day 16 (P16), the calyx terminal exhibits a fenestrated morphology that is considered mature in morphology and function.
source: By P12, the calyx terminal begins a change to a fenestrated morphology that is prevalent by P16, when it is considered to be mature in morphology and function (Grande and Wang, 2011) (Figure 1B, right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Grande and Wang, 2011, and shown in Figure 1B right panels.

claim: 5.8S ribosomal RNA is present in the calyx of Held presynaptic nerve terminal.
source: Immunolabeling of 5.8S rRNA identifies ribosomes. White arrows in each panel depict some examples of clear presynaptic 5.8S rRNA signal.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunolabeling shown in Figure 1C and 1D with white arrows marking presynaptic 5.8S rRNA signal.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between VGLUT1 and 5.8S rRNA signals in the presynaptic terminal is 0.78 ± 0.02.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) quantifies colocalization between the VGLUT1 and 5.8S rRNA signals, (n = 13 presynaptic terminals). The r-value of 0.78 ± 0.02, demonstrates high colocalization.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between VGLUT1 and 5.8S rRNA signals in the postsynaptic cell body region is 0.11 ± 0.10.
source: The r-values for the matching postsynaptic cell body regions (n = 13) have an r-value of 0.11 ± 0.10 (p ≤ 0.001 t-test and KS2-test; AD-test for presynaptic dataset normal distribution, p = 0.06).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 1F as a control comparison.

claim: Nuclease treatment prior to 5.8S rRNA antibody binding eliminates the ribosomal signal.
source: Nuclease treatment prior to 5.8S rRNA antibody binding eliminates the ribosomal signal. Enhanced contrast further shows the lack of ribosomal RNA after nuclease treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and quantified in Figure 1H, demonstrating specificity of the antibody.

claim: Nuclease treatment effectively eliminates 5.8S rRNA signal compared to control conditions (p ≤ 0.001).
source: Nuclease treatment effectively eliminates 5.8S rRNA signal compared to control conditions (p ≤ 0.001 t-test and KS2-test; AD-test control dataset normal distribution, p = 0.025).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison shown in Figure 1H demonstrating antibody specificity.

claim: Active translation occurs in calyx of Held nerve terminals as demonstrated by puromycin incorporation.
source: VGLUT1 antibody identifies the presynaptic terminal by labeling synaptic vesicles in the calyx of Held nerve terminal. Puromycin, tRNA analog, labeling shows active translation sites (SUnSET). Merge VGLUT1 +Puromycin shows active presynaptic ribosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated using the SUnSET technique shown in Figure 2A with puromycin labeling colocalizing with VGLUT1.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between VGLUT1 and puromycin signals in presynaptic terminals is 0.74 ± 0.05.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) quantifies colocalization between VGLUT1 and puromycin signals for presynaptic terminals (n = 13). Average r = 0.74 ± 0.05, demonstrates high colocalization.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of colocalization reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between VGLUT1 and puromycin signals in postsynaptic cell bodies is 0.14 ± 0.03.
source: A comparison, average r in corresponding postsynaptic cell bodies = 0.14 ± 0.03 (p ≤ 0.001 t-test and KS2-test; AD-test presynaptic dataset normal distribution, p = 0.06, AD-test postsynaptic dataset normal distribution, p = 0.05; n = 13).
evidence: This is a control measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Anisomycin treatment for 1 hour prior to puromycin application eliminates puromycin labeling.
source: Application of translational inhibitor (anisomycin, 40 μM) for 1 hr prior to puromycin treatment eliminates puromycin labeling (center panel and right panel), showing specificity of puromycin binding to active ribosomes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and quantified in Figure 2E, demonstrating that puromycin specifically labels active translation.

claim: Anisomycin treatment reduces puromycin signal by more than 100-fold compared to control.
source: Anisomycin treatment eliminates the puromycin signal. Inset shows higher detail of the residual ROI pixel intensity following anisomycin treatment (Pixel Intensity Ctrl = 64.4 ± 1.76, Aniso = 0.14 ± 0.02; p ≤ 0.001 t-test and KS2-test; n = 10).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2E showing a reduction from 64.4 to 0.14 pixel intensity.

claim: The initial mEPSC frequency is higher in cells treated with anisomycin (2.4 ± 0.7 Hz) compared to untreated neurons (1.4 ± 0.3 Hz).
source: We find that the initial mEPSC frequency, measured shortly after onset of whole-cell recording, is higher in cells treated with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin (2.4 ± 0.7 Hz, n = 11 cells) compared to untreated neurons (1.4 ± 0.3 Hz, n = 10 cells) from the same animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of spontaneous release frequency reported in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis decreases the time between mEPSC events compared to control recordings (p < 0.001).
source: The initial cumulative probability histogram of the time between mEPSC events clearly shows that inhibiting protein synthesis decreases the time between mEPSC events compared to control recordings of neurons in untreated slices from the same animals (Figure 3B, p < 0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of cumulative probability distributions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In anisomycin-treated neurons, 70% of mEPSC events occur with an interval less than ~350 msec, compared to ~700 msec for control recordings.
source: For example, in neurons treated with anisomycin, 70 percent of the events occur with an interval less than ~350 msec (Figure 3B, red dotted line), compared to ~700 msec for control recordings (Figure 3B, black dotted line).
evidence: This is derived from the cumulative probability analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fast component of spontaneous release accounts for 64% of mEPSC events in anisomycin-treated neurons and 37% in control neurons.
source: Interestingly, the fast component of the exponential fit, which corresponds to shorter event intervals, accounts for the majority of mEPSC events for anisomycin treated neurons (64%), in contrast to control neurons where the brief event intervals only account for 37% of the mEPSC event intervals.
evidence: This is derived from double exponential fits to the cumulative probability data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amplitudes of mEPSCs are similar for control (36.8 ± 2.5 pA) and protein synthesis inhibited neurons (38.7 ± 2.0 pA).
source: In contrast to the differences seen in the frequency of mEPSCs, the amplitudes of mEPSCs were similar for control (36.8 ± 2.5 pA, n = 10 cells) and protein synthesis inhibited neurons (38.7 ± 2.0 pA, n = 11 cells), as shown in the cumulative probability of the mEPSC amplitudes (Figure 3C) and the amplitude histogram (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mEPSC rise time, decay time, and average area show no statistically significant differences between control and protein synthesis inhibited neurons.
source: For the shape of the mEPSCs, the protein synthesis inhibited neurons have a similar rise time (Figure 3D, p = 0.19 t-test; 0.57 KS2-test; AD-test control data normal distribution p = 0.06), decay time (Figure 3D, p = 0.14 t-test; 0.54 KS2-test), and average mEPSC area (Figure 3E, p = 0.16 t-test; 0.29 KS2-test) with no statistically significant differences between them.
evidence: These are statistical comparisons of mEPSC shape parameters shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Following tetanic stimulation, the frequency of spontaneous release is nearly identical for control (6.1 ± 0.86 Hz) and protein synthesis inhibited neurons (6.9 ± 1.2 Hz).
source: Interestingly, following tetanic stimulation, the frequency of spontaneous release is nearly identical for both control (6.1 ± 0.86 Hz) and protein synthesis inhibited (6.9 ± 1.2 Hz) neurons (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This is a direct measurement of spontaneous release frequency after tetanic stimulation reported in the text and shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: Following tetanic stimulation, the cumulative probability distributions of mEPSC intervals for control and protein synthesis inhibited neurons partially overlap with no statistically significant difference (p = 0.35).
source: This is best shown in the cumulative probability histogram of the mEPSC intervals, where the control and protein synthesis inhibited mEPSC curves partially overlap, and no longer have a statistically significant difference (Figure 4B2, p = 0.35, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of cumulative probability distributions shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: The 10-90% rise time of evoked EPSCs is similar for control and anisomycin treated neurons (p = 0.43).
source: Average 10–90% evoked EPSC rise time for control (black) and anisomycin (red) treated neurons (p = 0.43 t-test; 0.96 KS2-test; n = 9 control, eight anisomycin).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of EPSC rise times shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 10-90% decay time of evoked EPSCs is similar for control and anisomycin treated neurons (p = 0.15).
source: Average 10–90% evoked EPSC decay time for control (black) and anisomycin (red) treated neurons (p = 0.15 t-test; 0.28 KS2-test; n = 9 control, eight anisomycin).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of EPSC decay times shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The latency of evoked EPSCs is similar for control and anisomycin treated neurons (p = 0.52).
source: Average evoked EPSC latency for control (black) and anisomycin (red) treated neurons. (p = 0.52 t-test; 0.69 KS2-test; n = 9 control, eight anisomycin).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of EPSC latencies shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The peak amplitude of initial evoked EPSCs is decreased in anisomycin treated cells (4.05 ± 0.64 pA) compared to control (6.21 ± 0.41 pA) with p = 0.013 by t-test.
source: However, there is a decrease in the peak amplitude of the initial evoked responses (Figure 5E) in control (6.21 ± 0.41 pA, n = 8) and anisomycin treated cells (4.05 ± 0.64 pA; n = 8; p = 0.013 t-test; p = 0.092 KS2-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of EPSC amplitudes shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The area of initial evoked EPSCs is decreased in anisomycin treated cells (4.26 ± 0.94 pA) compared to control (6.75 ± 0.54 nA·msec) with p = 0.04.
source: However, consistent with a reduction in the peak response, we find a difference in the area of the response (Figure 5F) in control (6.75 ± 0.54 nA·msec, n = 8) and anisomycin treated cells (4.26 ± 0.94 pA; n = 8; p = 0.04; p = 0.01 KS2-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of EPSC areas shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At a 5 msec interpulse interval, control cells show paired pulse depression (0.72 ± 0.07) while translation inhibited cells show facilitation (1.09 ± 0.09) with p = 0.004.
source: We find paired pulse depression at an interpulse interval (IPI) of 5 msec in control cells (0.72 ± 0.07 SEM, n = 9 cells from seven animals) but a facilitation in translation inhibited cells at the same interval (1.09 ± 0.09 SEM; p = 0.004 t-test; p = 0.006 KS2 test; n = 8 cells from six animals).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of paired pulse ratios shown in Figure 6A2.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis with anisomycin reduces depression throughout a 400 msec train at 200 Hz stimulation compared to control neurons (p < 0.001 ANOVA).
source: Consistent with the paired pulse results, we observe a reduced level of depression throughout the train of EPSCs after inhibiting protein synthesis with anisomycin compared to the response from control neurons. Accordingly, we directly compared the average responses for the entire train and found that the reduced depression seen after inhibiting protein synthesis occurred throughout the 400 msec train at 200 Hz (Figure 6B2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B2 with statistical comparison by ANOVA.

claim: At a 10 msec interpulse interval, control recordings show paired pulse depression (0.50 ± 0.06) while protein synthesis inhibited responses show only weak depression (0.93 ± 0.06) with p < 0.001.
source: At this interval, additional depression occurred in control recordings (0.50 ± 0.06 SEM, n = 8 cells from seven animals) but protein synthesis inhibited responses exhibited only weak depression (0.93 ± 0.06 SEM, n = 8 cells from seven animals; p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of paired pulse ratios at 10 msec IPI shown in Figure 6C2.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis with emetine increases the paired pulse ratio at 5 msec IPI from 0.56 ± 0.1 in control to 0.78 ± 0.1 (p = 0.03).
source: At an interval of 5 msec, the paired pulse ratio increased from 0.56 ± 0.1 SEM in control recordings to 0.78 ± 0.1 SEM after treatment with emetine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B; p = 0.03, paired t-test; p = 0.03 WSR test; emetine AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.03; seven control recordings paired with seven emetine recordings; seven mice total).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison using a different protein synthesis inhibitor shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis reduces depression during 100 Hz stimulation compared to control responses (p < 0.001 ANOVA).
source: Similar to the results at a five msec IPI (200 Hz), we find inhibiting protein synthesis by treatment with anisomycin reduced depression at 100 Hz compared to control responses (Figure 6D1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D1 with statistical comparison by ANOVA.

claim: The average P1 amplitude is smaller for anisomycin treated neurons (4.61 ± 0.59) compared to controls (6.85 ± 0.59) with p = 0.015.
source: In agreement with this, we note that the average P1 amplitude is smaller for anisomycin treated neurons (4.61 ± 0.59 SEM) compared to controls (6.85 ± 0.59 SEM; p = 0.015; Figure 6D2).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of first pulse amplitudes shown in Figure 6D2.

claim: The readily releasable pool (RRP) size is the same for control neurons (16.3 ± 1.6 nA) and protein synthesis inhibited neurons (15.97 ± 1.9 nA) at 100 Hz stimulation (p = 0.89).
source: Using this method, the average size of the RRP (Figure 7A2) was the same for control neurons (16.3 ± 1.6 nA, n = 9 control and eight anisomycin cells) and protein synthesis inhibited neurons (anisomycin, 15.97 ± 1.9 nA, n = 8 from seven animals; p = 0.89 t-test; 0.88 KS2-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of RRP measurements shown in Figure 7A2.

claim: The initial release probability (Pr) at 100 Hz is higher for control neurons (0.44 ± 0.03) than anisomycin treated neurons (0.29 ± 0.02) with p = 0.003.
source: Next, we find the initial release probability (Pr) for control neurons (0.44 ± 0.03) is higher than the value in anisomycin treated neurons (0.29 ± 0.02; p = 0.003 t-test; p = 0.006 KS2-test), therefore the differences we see in the initial peak response in protein synthesis inhibited neurons is explained by a reduction in the initial probability of release (Figure 7A3).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of initial release probability shown in Figure 7A3.

claim: The rate of vesicle replenishment at 100 Hz increases when protein synthesis is inhibited (96.9 ± 1.6 pA/msec) compared to control neurons (62.2 ± 3.5 pA/msec) with p = 0.037.
source: We find that the rate of vesicle replenishment (Figure 7A4) increases when protein synthesis is inhibited (96.9 ± 1.6 pA/msec), compared to the rate in control neurons (62.2 ± 3.5 pA/msec; p = 0.037 t-test; p = 0.041 KS2-test; control data AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of vesicle replenishment rates shown in Figure 7A4.

claim: The readily releasable pool (RRP) size at 200 Hz is the same for control neurons (16.8 ± 1.5 nA) and anisomycin treated neurons (16.8 ± 2.6 nA) with p > 0.99.
source: At 200 Hz, the RRP-value for control neurons is 16.8 ± 1.5 nA, which matches the RRP-value for anisomycin treated neurons (16.8 ± 2.6 nA; p > 0.99 t-test; 0.88 KS2-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of RRP measurements at 200 Hz shown in Figure 7B2.

claim: The initial probability of release at 200 Hz is 0.43 ± 0.02 for control and 0.3 ± 0.03 for anisomycin treated neurons (p = 0.005).
source: As expected, the initial probability of release at 200 Hz is nearly identical to the values measured at 100 Hz stimulation (Figure 7A3), with a Pr of 0.43 ± 0.02 for control and 0.3 ± 0.03 for anisomycin treated neurons (p = 0.005 t-test; p = 0.006 KS2-test; anisomycin AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.08) estimated from the EPSC responses generated by 200 Hz stimulation (Figure 7 B3).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of initial release probability at 200 Hz shown in Figure 7B3.

claim: At 200 Hz, anisomycin treated neurons maintain a faster rate of vesicle replenishment (154.1 ± 23.4 pA/msec) compared to control neurons (102.8 ± 5.9 pA/msec) with p = 0.04.
source: At 200 Hz, the anisomycin treated neurons maintained a faster rate of replenishment (154.1 ± 23.4 pA/msec) compared to control neurons at 200 Hz (102.8 ± 5.9 pA/msec; p = 0.04 t-test and KS2-test; control data AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.053).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of vesicle replenishment rates at 200 Hz shown in Figure 7B4.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis with emetine decreases the probability of release at 100 Hz from 0.46 ± 0.07 in controls to 0.33 ± 0.06 (p = 0.036).
source: At 100 Hz, Pr decreases from 0.46 ± 0.07 SEM in controls to 0.33 ± 0.06 SEM (p = 0.036 paired t-test; 0.047 Wilcoxon Signed Rank-test; emetine AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.01; n = 7 for each condition; seven mice) after inhibiting protein synthesis with emetine (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison using emetine shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibiting protein synthesis with emetine decreases the probability of release at 200 Hz from 0.47 ± 0.06 in controls to 0.36 ± 0.05 (p = 0.046).
source: A similar reduction in Pr is seen with 200 Hz stimulation, where the Pr under control conditions was 0.47 ± 0.06 SEM, and decreased to 0.36 ± 0.05 SEM (p = 0.046 paired t-test; p = 0.031 WSR-test; emetine AD-test for normal distribution p = 0.01; n = 7 for each condition; seven mice) after inhibiting protein synthesis with emetine (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison using emetine at 200 Hz shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The calyx of Held synapse is involved in sound localization and can maintain prolonged synaptic transmission at frequencies of 100 to 200 Hz.
source: This synapse is involved in sound localization, and can maintain prolonged synaptic transmission at frequencies of 100 to 200 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the properties of the calyx of Held synapse.

claim: The calyx of Held is a large, glutamatergic nerve terminal that forms a monosynaptic, axosomatic connection onto MNTB principle cells.
source: The calyx of Held is a large, glutamatergic nerve terminal that forms a monosynaptic, axosomatic connection onto MNTB principle cells.
evidence: This is a description of the synapse stated in the Introduction.

claim: The calyx of Held nerve terminal contains hundreds of individual release sites.
source: This large presynaptic terminal contains hundreds of individual release sites, and the size of the terminal facilitates imaging (Rodríguez-Contreras et al., 2008; Körber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In a mouse brain, the calyx of Held nerve terminal is approximately 3 mm away from the cell body.
source: Finally, in a mouse brain, the calyx of Held nerve terminal is ~3 mm away from the cell body.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction describing the anatomical distance.

claim: 5.8S rRNA is a major component of the eukaryotic ribosome which is required to execute ribosomal translocation.
source: To investigate presynaptic protein synthesis, we first determined whether 5.8S ribosomal RNA (rRNA), a major component of the eukaryotic ribosome which is required to execute ribosomal translocation (Lerner et al., 1981; Abou Elela and Nazar, 1997; Koenig et al., 2000), is present in the nerve terminal.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the functional role of 5.8S rRNA.

claim: 5.8S rRNA is part of the large 80S ribosomal subunit and is eukaryotic specific.
source: This component is eukaryotic specific and part of the large 80S ribosomal subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the properties of 5.8S rRNA.

claim: The 5.8S rRNA antibody does not label mitochondrial ribosomes which are more prokaryotic in their composition.
source: Therefore, this antibody does not label mitochondrial ribosomes which are more prokaryotic in their composition.
evidence: This is stated to explain the specificity of the antibody used.

claim: VGLUT1 antibody labels most of the presynaptic compartment by marking glutamatergic synaptic vesicles.
source: To label the large calyx of Held nerve terminal, an antibody against the vesicular glutamate transporter, VGLUT1, was used (Figure 1C,D; left panel, green), which labels most of the presynaptic compartment by marking glutamatergic synaptic vesicles (Billups, 2005; Rodríguez-Contreras et al., 2008; Fioravante et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Kempf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the use of VGLUT1 as a presynaptic marker.

claim: The average intensity ratio for the presynaptic terminal to background signal for 5.8S rRNA is 3:1.
source: In the region shown here, the average intensity ratio for the presynaptic terminal to background signal is 3:1, which allowed us to clearly distinguish the presynaptic signal.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of signal intensity reported in the Results.

claim: The average intensity ratio for somata to presynaptic signals for 5.8S rRNA is 4:1.
source: As expected, the average intensity for the signal in the presynaptic terminal was less than that of the somata, with an average intensity ratio of 4:1 for somata to presynaptic signals.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of signal intensities reported in the Results.

claim: The SUnSET technique uses puromycin, which mimics tRNA and becomes incorporated into nascent polypeptide chains.
source: Briefly, this method uses puromycin, which mimics tRNA and becomes incorporated into nascent polypeptide chains.
evidence: This is a description of the SUnSET technique stated in the Results.

claim: Puromycin must be incorporated into a polypeptide chain to be detected by the SUnSET assay, requiring ribosomes to be active.
source: Ribosomes must be active for puromycin to be incorporated into a polypeptide chain to be detected by the SUnSET assay.
evidence: This is stated to explain the specificity of the SUnSET assay for active translation.

claim: Anisomycin specifically inhibits eukaryotic translation.
source: An important point is that anisomycin specifically inhibits eukaryotic translation.
evidence: This is stated to explain the specificity of anisomycin as a translational inhibitor.

claim: Mitochondrial protein synthesis does not contribute to the active ribosome signal measured by the SUnSET assay.
source: We conclude that the complete loss of SUnSET signal that was induced by anisomycin treatment shows that mitochondrial protein synthesis does not contribute to the active ribosome signal we see here.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that anisomycin completely eliminates the puromycin signal.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous events is due to presynaptic release properties.
source: The frequency of spontaneous events is due to presynaptic release properties (Kavalali, 2015) while the amplitude and shape of the response are largely attributed to postsynaptic changes in ionotropic receptor responses.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the interpretation of mEPSC frequency.

claim: The amplitude and shape of mEPSC responses are largely attributed to postsynaptic changes in ionotropic receptor responses.
source: The frequency of spontaneous events is due to presynaptic release properties (Kavalali, 2015) while the amplitude and shape of the response are largely attributed to postsynaptic changes in ionotropic receptor responses.
evidence: This is stated to explain the interpretation of mEPSC amplitude and shape.

claim: Presynaptic properties such as the level of neurotransmitter filling in vesicles can affect the amplitude of the postsynaptic current.
source: However, presynaptic properties such as the level of neurotransmitter filling in vesicles can also affect the amplitude of the postsynaptic current (Goh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to acknowledge that presynaptic factors can also influence mEPSC amplitude.

claim: Ongoing protein synthesis acts to lower the spontaneous release frequency by favoring longer inter-event intervals.
source: Therefore, ongoing protein synthesis limits spontaneous release by favoring longer inter-event intervals.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that inhibiting protein synthesis increases the frequency of spontaneous release.

claim: Spontaneous release of glutamate can suppress local protein synthesis in dendrites.
source: For example, spontaneous release of glutamate can suppress local protein synthesis in dendrites (Sutton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for the importance of spontaneous release.

claim: NMDA receptors that are specifically activated by spontaneous release appear to be responsible for the rapid antidepressant effect produced by ketamine exposure.
source: Furthermore, NMDA receptors that are specifically activated by spontaneous release appear to be responsible for the rapid antidepressant effect produced by ketamine exposure (Autry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for the functional importance of spontaneous release.

claim: Vesicles that undergo spontaneous release may preferentially come from a population separate from the vesicles that respond to evoked release.
source: In addition, vesicles that undergo spontaneous release may preferentially come from a population separate from the vesicles that respond to evoked release (Sara et al., 2005), and this appears to involve association with specific proteins (Hua et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to provide context for the mechanisms of spontaneous release.

claim: Tetanic stimulation has been shown to transiently increase the frequency of spontaneous release, due to residual calcium.
source: Tetanic stimulation has previously been shown to transiently increase the frequency of spontaneous release, due to residual calcium (Korogod et al., 2005) and may also involve PKC activation (Korogod et al., 2007; Fioravante et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to provide context for the effects of tetanic stimulation.

claim: Inhibiting myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) at the calyx of Held causes an increase in the rate of spontaneous release.
source: For example, inhibiting myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) at the calyx of Held causes an increase in the rate of spontaneous release (Srinivasan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for other factors that affect spontaneous release.

claim: shRNA knockdown of Mover in the calyx of Held nerve terminal results in an increase in the probability of release.
source: shRNA knockdown experiments of a vertebrate-specific protein, Mover, in the calyx of Held nerve terminal results in an increase in the probability of release. This demonstrates that expression of specific presynaptic proteins can negatively or positively influence synaptic release probability (Körber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for how specific proteins can modulate release probability.

claim: MLCK inhibition causes an initial increase in the amplitude of EPSCs during high frequency stimulation, which appears to involve changes in the size of the readily releasable pool.
source: Interestingly, in addition to affecting spontaneous release, MLCK inhibition has also been shown to cause an initial increase in the amplitude of EPSCs during high frequency stimulation, although this appears to involve changes in the size of the readily releasable pool (Srinivasan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to compare with the current findings.

claim: The shape and amplitude of spontaneous and evoked responses are unaffected during the 1-2 hr that protein synthesis is inhibited.
source: Importantly, the shape and amplitude of spontaneous and evoked responses are unaffected during the 1–2 hr that protein synthesis is inhibited in our experiments, indicating that the postsynaptic receptor responses are not affected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the findings from the Results section.

claim: The lack of change in postsynaptic membrane currents argues against a possible retrograde signal that is affected by inhibiting protein synthesis.
source: The lack of change in the postsynaptic membrane currents also argues against a possible retrograde signal that is affected by inhibiting protein synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that postsynaptic responses are unchanged.

claim: In experiments where the postsynaptic neuron was lysed and removed, presynaptic release properties were not changed.
source: In support of this, in experiments where the postsynaptic neuron was lysed and removed, presynaptic release properties were not changed (He et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the conclusion that retrograde signaling is not involved.

claim: A majority of synaptic proteins have a half-life of approximately 36 hours.
source: There is evidence that a majority of synaptic proteins have a half-life of ~36 hr (Cohen and Ziv, 2017) however the techniques used to measure turnover may not be sensitive enough to capture proteins with a faster turnover rate that could compose a small but functionally important population of presynaptic proteins.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for protein turnover rates.

claim: Treatment of neurons with activity blockers results in a decrease of approximately 50% in the polyubiquitinated profile of proteins localized in post-synaptic density (PSD) fractions.
source: For example, it has been shown that treatment of neurons with activity blockers results in a decrease of ~50% in the polyubiquitinated profile of proteins localized in post-synaptic density (PSD) fractions, whereas treatment of neurons with activity inducers resulted in an increase in polyubiquitinated proteins (Ehlers, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to provide context for activity-dependent protein degradation.

claim: The transient rate of axoplasmic transport has been reported to be approximately 1 μm/sec in calyx of Held axons.
source: The transient rate of axoplasmic transport has been reported to ~1 μm/sec in calyx of Held axons (Wimmer et al., 2004), and sustained rates are much slower (Maday et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to provide context for the speed of axonal transport.

claim: Presynaptic transcripts code for a variety of proteins including some that can affect vesicle replenishment and fusion such as β-catenin, β-tubulin, and β-actin.
source: These presynaptic transcripts code for a variety of proteins including some that can affect vesicle replenishment and fusion such as β-catenin, β-tubulin, and β-actin.
evidence: This is stated to provide context for the types of proteins that could be synthesized locally.

claim: In the experiments, the calyx nerve terminal is no longer connected to the neuronal cell body because the axons are severed during brain slicing.
